query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding reactive elements like Y or Ce to refractory high-entropy alloys will improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: adding 1 at.% of Y or Ce to the alloy composition
generation.conditions: exposure to air at 1000°C for 100 hours
generation.structural_mediator: formation of a continuous and dense oxide layer
generation.mechanism: the added reactive elements scavenge oxygen and form a protective oxide layer, reducing the diffusion of oxygen into the alloy and thereby improving its high-temperature oxygen resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: a 30% reduction in weight gain due to oxidation compared to the untreated alloy
generation.baseline: untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exposed to air at 1000°C for 100 hours
generation.boundary: the improvement in high-temperature oxygen resistance will be significant at temperatures above 900°C
generation.uncertainty: the exact amount of improvement may vary depending on the specific alloy composition and the exposure conditions

falsification_experiment.design: expose the alloy with and without the added reactive elements to air at 1000°C for 100 hours and measure the weight gain due to oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the weight gain due to oxidation of the alloy with the added reactive elements is not at least 20% less than that of the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Cross-Sectional Morphology of The Oxide Film
cited_evidence.text: Figure 8 presents line scanning energy spectrum diagrams of the cross section of the AlTiNiCuCo1.0 alloy oxide layer after oxidation for 50 and 100 h at 800 °C. After 100 h oxidation, the oxide film was thicker than that after 50 h, but the change in thickness was not apparent. This indicates that the oxide film of an HEA of this composition under high-temperature oxidation is relatively dense and plays a certain protective role for the alloy; thus, the alloy has better high-temperature oxidation resistance. It can be seen from Figure 8a, representing 50 h oxidation, that the oxide layer still contained large amounts of Al, Ti, and O elements. It was presumed that there were mainly two oxides, Al2O3 and TiO2, in the oxide layer. After oxidation for 100 h, the contents of Al and Ti in the oxide layer were greater, and the content of Co was significantly increased. Combining this with XRD analysis results, it was found that there were three oxides present: CoAl2O4, Al2O3, and TiO2.

Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
